### 3. Review the task

Part of [SKILL.md](SKILL.md); the rules there hold in this step.

Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the
final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a
report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both
required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are
needed. Note the task's effective risk tier as you go (see Risk Tiers
in [SKILL.md](SKILL.md)) — the Claude task review always runs, but the tier decides whether
step 5's per-task Codex gate does.

- Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's
  `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` — it prints
  `wrote <path>: <N> commit(s), <N> bytes`, so take the path from that line
  and pass it to the reviewer (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`,
  `git diff --stat`, and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one
  uniquely named file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees
  the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read
  call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer —
  never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never
  dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file.
- **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief
  file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global
  constraints that bind the task. Write those global constraints to a small
  file alongside the brief and report: the per-task Codex gate takes the
  same file as its global-constraints handoff.
- The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention
  lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global
  Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the
  stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches
  Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI,
  test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS
  project's spec demands.
- Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests
  if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason
- Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the
  same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence
- Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to
  ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a
  false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review
  loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X
  as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are
  pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop. When the plan supplies
  example code, weaknesses in that code are fair review targets — the example
  was a starting point, not evidence that its weaknesses were chosen.

Append `Task <N>: review <approved|blocking> <reviewer id> <one line>` when a
task review or scoped re-review returns.

The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements
that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the
review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task
complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer
lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec
review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings.

Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md)

**Codex Review Gate (Claude Code only).** When running under Claude Code, add
a Codex **code** review gate at two points — here, per task, and once more
at the final whole-branch review — following
[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md).
Probe once per skill run and reuse the result; if Codex is absent, emit the
no-Codex notice once and run both gates as no-ops.

- **Per task:** after the task reviewer approves (spec ✅ and quality approved) and
  before marking the task complete, run the gate (standard/high effective tiers; an effective-low task skips it per Risk Tiers in [SKILL.md](SKILL.md), recording the tier-skip event instead) using the per-task code recipe
  with `--base <the task BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer>`.
  Provide the task brief path, implementer report path, review-package path, and
  the global-constraints file you wrote in step 3. The gate's dossier `--adjudications` inputs carry the plan's `**Spec:**` file path beside any spec-gate ledger, so the reviewer is handed the binding authority instead of inferring it.
- **Rounds are shared, not stacked.** Blocking findings from this gate enter
  the five-round loop in [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md), at the next round number — the gate has no
  separate Codex ceiling of its own. The task's fix-round budget is five,
  shared across Claude-reviewer rounds and Codex-gate rounds. Three mechanics
  keep that single budget honest:

  1. **One `GATE_DIR` for this task's whole gate lifecycle.** Create it at
     the task's first gate invocation and reuse that same dir for every
     Codex re-round of this task — the gate doc's §3 contract, "Use one
     `GATE_DIR` for the whole gate." `gate-round`'s counter lives in that
     dir, so it counts exactly this task's gate rounds and nothing else.
     When the `GATE_DIR` is first created, record it in the progress ledger
     as one line `Task N gate dir: <path>`; on resume (or any later Codex
     re-round), reuse the ledgered path instead of creating a new one; if
     the ledgered dir no longer exists (cache purged), treat the task's
     prior gate rounds as unknown and fail closed: do not assume zero —
     reconstruct the consumed-round count from the ledger's fix-round
     entries and, if gate rounds cannot be established, surface via BLOCKED
     rather than restarting the count. After each gate round, append
     `Task <N>: codex gate round <R> <approved|blocking> <one line>`, R being
     the gate's own round number.
  2. **Let the counter do the arithmetic.** `gate-round` compares its LOCAL
     count — gate rounds only, monotonic within the `GATE_DIR` — against a
     ceiling, so the ceiling must leave gate rounds out; they are already in
     that count. Pass `--consumed <NON-gate fix rounds this task has consumed
     so far>` (all fix/re-review rounds, whatever the finding's origin — the
     gate's own invocation rounds are excluded only because `gate-round`'s
     counter already holds them) and the script derives the ceiling from the
     shared five-round cap itself. Recompute the consumed count at each call:
     non-gate rounds may land between gate rounds. Do not hand-compute
     `--ceiling` for a task gate — that is how twenty measured task gates
     recorded ceilings of 1, 2, 6, and 7, two of which the cap makes
     impossible. `--consumed` cannot express them.
  3. **A spent cap is BLOCKED, not a gate round.** When the task's consumed
     rounds already total five, `--consumed 5` yields a ceiling of zero and
     the gate backstops on its first call. That is the fail-closed floor, not
     the intended path: check before calling, and when the cap is spent follow
     the breaker in [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md) and surface the task as BLOCKED rather than spending a
     gate invocation to learn it.

  The invariant in one line: **local gate rounds + non-gate fix rounds ≤ 5**,
  enforced because `gate-round` blocks (verdict `backstop`) the moment its
  local count would exceed the ceiling. Count every round the
  gate runs against the task's shared budget — each gate round consumes one
  of the five, exactly like a reviewer round. After a Codex-triggered fix,
  the scoped re-review verifies it; the gate re-runs only once that
  re-review verdicts every finding ADDRESSED or DECLINED.

### 5. Complete the task

When the review comes back clean — the task reviewer approved, every
fix-loop finding is addressed or declined, and the per-task Codex gate
approved or was skipped by tier — in this order, each step idempotent on a
resume:

- Append `Task <N>: approved <full id>` with the head the reviewers saw,
  written with `git rev-parse <head>` (every later approval of the same task
  appends a new line; the newest is what merges). merge-back compares the
  whole id, so a shortened id reads as no approval.
- Merge back: `scripts/sdd-state merge-back PLAN_FILE N --session <sid> --commit <sha>`.
  `merged` continues (`already=1` on a resume means the ref was moved
  before the crash). `conflict paths=<list>`: merge the integration branch
  into the task branch in your worktree (`git merge <integration>`), resolve
  through one implementer dispatch whose brief names the paths and both
  sides, re-run the task reviewer over the resolution and the task gate's
  re-review lens, append the new `approved` line, and retry. `checked-out`
  names a worktree or `lease:<sid>`: a final train holds the branch; post a
  `tasks` record and retry after it ends, or ask your human partner to move
  the checkout. `not-approved approved=<sha7|none>` means your bookkeeping
  is behind: the commit you passed is not the task's newest `approved` line,
  so append the `approved` line for the head the reviewers saw (or pass that
  head) and retry. `blocked waiting=<list>` (exit 7) means an amendment put a
  prerequisite under your claim after you took it, and merge-back enforces
  the edge: leave the `approved` line as it is, and never write a completion
  line for a task this session did not complete. Run `next` and take what it
  offers; on `own-blocked`, post, print the board and hand back as the
  `own-blocked` text in [task-loop.md](task-loop.md) says. Retry merge-back once every waiting task has
  its completion line, or after your human partner removes the edge.
  `not-holder owner=<sid>` (exit 4)
  means the claim is no longer yours (after a takeover your human partner
  granted, that session holds it): stop and hand back with the line; never
  repair the ledger or take the claim back.
- Detach at the merged head and drop the task branch:
  `git switch --detach <merged head>` then `git branch -d <task branch>`
  (its commits are on the integration branch now; a missing branch on a
  resume is fine). If `-d` refuses, the branch holds commits that were never
  approved or merged: keep it, do not force the delete, and hand back to
  your human partner with git's output.
- Complete the task: run `scripts/sdd-state complete PLAN_FILE N
  --commits <base7>..<head7>` and repeat it until it prints `status=complete`
  (`busy` and `error` are retried; `unknown-task` means the number is not a
  heading in the plan, `no-workspace` that the ledger is gone, and a usage
  error that the arguments are wrong: each of those stops you, not the loop).
  Its `snapshot=` is the completion's durable record.
- Mark the todo complete (where you keep todos), and run `next`.

A task whose ledger has a `merged` line and no completion line is resumed
at the completion line, never redispatched.

## Final Review

Part of [SKILL.md](SKILL.md); the rules there hold in this step.

The final train is claimed. When `next` says `complete`, run
`scripts/sdd-state claim PLAN_FILE final --session <sid>`: `claimed` means
this session runs the final review, the final gate and Finish; `blocked`
names tasks still open (claims without completion lines elsewhere: wait or
ask); `held` with your own session id (`own=1`, a resume after compaction)
means this session already holds the train: continue as its holder; `held`
names the session that holds it, or `lease=<sid> plan=<ws>`
when a sibling plan's final holds the branch: post a `tasks` record naming
the holder, print the board, and hand back. The holder checks the
integration branch out in its own worktree (`git switch <integration>`), the
one time a session does so, and runs the review package, the final
reviewer, the fix wave and the final Codex gate on it; its fix commits land
on the integration branch directly, which the lease makes safe.

Once you hold the train and have checked the integration branch out, the
final whole-branch review gets a package too: run
`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the
branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) — take the path from the
`wrote <path>: ...` line and include it in the final review dispatch, so the
final reviewer reads one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git
commands. Dispatch
on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using
hyperpowers:requesting-code-review's
[code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at
the ledger's deferred-minor lines — and at `tier-skips.md`, if any task
skipped its per-task gate — so it can triage which must be fixed before
merge.

If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent
with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding. Compose the
dispatch from [fix-subagent-prompt.md](fix-subagent-prompt.md).
Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real
session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined.
Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave
(`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range,
[re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) using its Final-wave usage note).
There is no second fix wave: anything the re-review leaves open — and any
finding that conflicts with the plan's text — goes to your human partner
with the evidence, as BLOCKED, when finishing-a-development-branch presents
the options.

**Dispatch the decision extractor.** When the ledger has a `Decisions listing:`
line (and otherwise nothing), once the fix wave and its re-review are
clean (or the final review returned no findings), take a scratch directory
from `../requesting-code-review/scripts/codex-review-dir`, regenerate the
full-branch package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD`, so a
fix wave's commits are in it) and copy it and `<workspace>/progress.md` into
it, and dispatch the
extractor in the background, composed from
`../finishing-a-development-branch/decision-notes-prompt.md` with those two
copies, the plan, the spec, the `Decisions listing:` from the ledger, the
index (`decisions/README.md` beside the spec's directory) when it exists, and
`<dir>/decision-notes.md` as its output path. Record it in the ledger:
`Decision extractor: <task id> -> <dir>/decision-notes.md`. The dispatch is
complete only when that line is in the ledger: write it before any other tool
call, because after a compaction it is the only record of the task id and the
notes path, and without it a resumed controller can neither collect nor stop
the extractor. The extractor reads nothing inside the workspace, so Finish may
delete the workspace while it runs;
finishing-a-development-branch collects it after the full suite and never
waits for it, and neither do you. On a harness with no tracked background
subagent, skip the dispatch and note it in the ledger. If a Codex final-gate
fix changes code after the dispatch: stop the extractor (TaskStop); when the
fix altered one of the spec's decisions, settle that first (show your human
partner the change you would write into the `## Decisions` item, write and
commit it on the branch with their approval; without it the item stands and
the change is raised again at the menu); re-run the dry run and replace the
ledger's `Decisions listing:`; regenerate the full-branch package and copy
it, with the current `<workspace>/progress.md`, into the scratch directory,
replacing the earlier copies; compose the replacement dispatch from those
copies; then dispatch the extractor again and replace the
`Decision extractor:` line.

**Codex Review Gate — final whole-branch (Claude Code only).** After the final code-reviewer
subagent and its fix wave, and before hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch,
run the gate using the final whole-branch code recipe with `--base <branch
merge-base, e.g. git merge-base main HEAD>`. Provide the branch
review-package path, plan or requirements path, the Minor findings ledger if
present, and the tier-skip summary if any task skipped. The final dossier passes the plan's `**Spec:**` file as a `--doc` input beside the plan, and carries the tier-skip summary among its `--adjudications`. Resolve blocking
findings with one fix subagent carrying the complete list, per this
section's existing guidance, before finishing. After any Codex-triggered
final-review fix, re-run the final code-reviewer before re-running the final
Codex gate.

Unlike the per-task gate, the final gate keeps a ceiling of its own: the
gate's convergence stop-rule and per-gate backstop bound this loop (code
gates use a code-gate backstop of 3 rounds). If the backstop is hit with
unresolved blocking findings, surface them to your human partner rather than
looping.

## Finish

When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged:

1. **Read your session line** from the ledger (its `mode`), and copy the
   ledger's `Decisions listing:` and `Decision extractor:` lines (or its
   skip reason) into the hand-off message you are about to send: the next
   step removes the ledger from the working tree, and
   hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch takes the mode, the plan, the
   spec and the extractor's task id and output path as its input.
2. **Finish the workspace** with `scripts/sdd-state finish PLAN_FILE --session <sid>`:
   it refuses with `open-claims` while any claimed task lacks a completion line
   (that is a plan not finished, not a reason for `--force`), and with
   `busy` (exit 3) when another session is writing the workspace or a copy
   from an interrupted removal sits beside it (report the stderr line, wait
   for the other session or ask your human partner about the copy, then run
   `finish` again); it also refuses with `live-jobs` while a tracked job it
   names is still live (run `tracked-job wait` on it, or `tracked-job stop`
   when the job is no longer wanted, then run `finish` again). `not-holder`
   or `no-final-claim` (exit 11): this session does not hold the final
   train; stop and hand back. Otherwise it
   removes the plan's directory, commits the removal to the state branch,
   and prints `last=<sha>`, the commit that still holds the dossier,
   `push=<remote>/<branch>` and `receipt=<path>`, the durable copy of the
   ledger, the guard's log and the job records; record the receipt path in
   your closing message. A line reading `receipt=none staging=<path>` means
   the record exists only under that staging path: name the path to your
   human partner in the closing message. A space in either path prints as
   `%20`, so decode it before you name the path. On the plain backend it
   prints `backend=plain` instead of `last=` and `push=`, and there is
   nothing to push. `none` means there was no workspace to remove, and
   `error` (exit 2) that the removal or its commit failed: any status other
   than `finished` stops Finish until the command
   succeeds; show its stderr line.
3. **Verify deletion** with `test ! -d "<workspace>"` to confirm it is gone.
   The push command is `git -C <checkout> push <remote> <branch>`, the
   checkout being the parent of the `plans/` directory `sdd-dir` printed;
   run it only if your human partner asks.
4. **Keep the lease through the branch action.** `finish` leaves the branch
   lease in place; hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch marks the
   branch closing before a merge and releases the lease after whichever
   option your human partner chose. Hand it the plan path and your session
   id for that. When the final ends with a hand-back instead, detach your
   worktree first (`git switch --detach`) and then release the lease
   yourself, as the last action:
   `scripts/sdd-state lease PLAN_FILE --release --session <sid>`.

A clean finish that leaves the workspace behind is an INCOMPLETE finish —
"keeping it for reference" is not an option; the repo's commits are the
durable record. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them

---
name: subagent-driven-development
description: Use when executing implementation plans with independent tasks in the current session
---

# Subagent-Driven Development

Execute plan by dispatching a fresh implementer subagent per task, a task review (spec compliance + code quality) after each, and a broad whole-branch review at the end.

**Why subagents:** You delegate tasks to specialized agents with isolated context. By precisely crafting their instructions and context, you ensure they stay focused and succeed at their task. They should never inherit your session's context or history — you construct exactly what they need. This also preserves your own context for coordination work.

**Core principle:** Fresh subagent per task + task review (spec + quality) + broad final review = high quality, fast iteration

**Narration:** between tool calls, narrate at most one short line — the
ledger and the tool results carry the record.

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for anything you write to your human partner in this skill: the pre-flight question, an escalation, a BLOCKED hand-back.

**Continuous execution:** Do not pause to check in with your human partner between tasks. Execute all tasks from the plan without stopping. While the plan has tasks left, a turn ends in exactly three cases: a BLOCKED status you cannot resolve; a question only your human partner can answer, asked in that message (ambiguity that genuinely prevents progress is such a question); or, on a harness that cannot wait in the foreground, tracked work still running, named in that message. A message that names your next step is followed by that step's tool call in the same turn. "Tasks 1 and 2 are done. Moving to Task 3." followed by a turn end is a stop: your human partner reads it as work in progress, and nothing resumes it until they type. Completing the last task does not end the plan: it opens the final whole-branch review, and the plan ends only after Finish. Each permitted turn end, and "your human partner asked you to stop", is written to the ledger in the same message that ends the turn: run `scripts/sdd-state handback PLAN_FILE --reason "<why>"` (add `--session <sid>` on a harness without `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID`; `busy` or `error` is retried, and without the line the guard falls back to reading your last message). Write that line only for a question only your human partner can answer, a BLOCKED report, or their request to stop; finishing the tasks is never a reason for it. On Claude Code the SDD stop guard refuses a turn end it can prove is premature, two consecutive attempts per plan, the count resetting after any allow, with this message: "SDD stop guard: plan <plan path> is not finished (<state>; nothing tracked is live). Take the next step now, in this turn. If you are handing back to your human partner (a question only they can answer, a BLOCKED report, or they asked you to stop), run scripts/sdd-state handback PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --reason "<why>" and end the turn with that message." (with a live job the first sentences name the job and say to watch it with `tracked-job wait`). When you meet it, take the next step; writing a question you do not need answered to get past it is the stop it exists to prevent, and the log records every allow. "Should I continue?" prompts and progress summaries waste their time — they asked you to execute the plan, so execute it.

**Tracked work only:** anything that outlives one tool call starts through your harness's tracked background option (`run_in_background` on Claude Code); never start it with a trailing `&`, `nohup`, `setsid`, `disown`, or a script that detaches a process. The harness never reports on such a process, so nothing wakes you when it ends, and a turn you end to wait for it does not resume.

**After every context compaction:** this file fits within the 20,000 characters Claude Code re-attaches, so the copy you hold is whole. A step file you read before the compaction does not survive it. Before your next action, print the board and the ledger lines the step table names (your task's and your Setup's, never the whole ledger), find your step in the table, and Read that step file in full.

## When to Use

```dot
digraph when_to_use {
    "Have implementation plan?" [shape=diamond];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" [shape=diamond];
    "Stay in this session?" [shape=diamond];
    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];

    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];
    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
}
```

**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
- Same session (no context switch)
- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality), broad review at the end
- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)

## The Process

Each step's full text is in its own file beside this one. Read a step's file when you enter the step; after a compaction, the step table below names the one to read.

1. **Setup** ([setup.md](setup.md)): sync the state branch and find the plan's workspace, settle where the work happens (hyperpowers:using-git-worktrees), create or read the ledger and append your session line, verify, read the plan and the spec, run the pre-flight scan. Setup's last action appends `session <sid>: setup complete`.
2. **Take a task and dispatch** ([task-loop.md](task-loop.md)): `scripts/sdd-state next` offers a task; claim the first and switch to its branch (none to take, or blocked: post, print the board, hand back). Dispatch the implementer, answer its questions, handle its report.
3. **Review the task** ([review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md)): generate the review package and dispatch the task reviewer. Blocking findings go to step 4; a finding that conflicts with the plan text goes to your human partner first.
4. **Fix loop** ([fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md)): fix rounds, each with a scoped re-review, under the shared cap in the rules below. When no finding is left open, go back to review-and-complete.md for the gate.
5. **Codex task gate and completion** ([review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md)): unless the task's effective tier is low, run the per-task Codex gate (blocking findings re-enter step 4). Append the `approved` line, merge back, detach, delete the task branch, and run `scripts/sdd-state complete`; any status but `complete` stops. Then step 2.
6. **Final review and Finish** ([final-and-finish.md](final-and-finish.md)): when no task remains, claim the final train, dispatch the final reviewer (one fix dispatch, one scoped re-review), the decision extractor and the Codex final gate, delete the workspace, then use hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.

## After a compaction: the step table

Print the board (`scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE`) and the ledger lines of your task and your Setup (`grep -E '^(Task <N>:|session <sid>: setup complete)' <workspace>/progress.md`, leaving out `Task <N>:` when you hold no task); `scripts/sdd-dir PLAN_FILE` prints the workspace. Do not Read the whole ledger after a compaction: it grows with the plan. A row's newest line is the newest of your task's lines the table names (its branch, base, implementer identity, `report`, `review`, Codex gate round, `approved`, `merged` and `fix round` lines); a line it does not name, such as a deferred minor or the gate directory, leaves your step unchanged. Then Read the step file this table names:

| State | Step file |
|---|---|
| no ledger in the workspace, or no `setup complete` line of this session in it | [setup.md](setup.md) |
| the board shows no task held by this session and a task without a completion line | [task-loop.md](task-loop.md) |
| the held task's newest line is its branch, base, implementer identity or `report` line | [task-loop.md](task-loop.md) |
| its newest line is a `review` or Codex gate line approving it, an `approved` line or a `merged` line | [review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md) |
| its newest line is a `fix round` line, or a `review` or Codex gate line with blocking findings | [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md) |
| this session holds the final claim, or every task has a completion line | [final-and-finish.md](final-and-finish.md) |

A state the table does not cover reads [task-loop.md](task-loop.md), and you record that in the ledger.

The table reads these ledger lines, so write each one where its step says:

- `session <sid>: setup complete`, Setup's last action;
- `Task <N>: report <status> <one line>`, after an implementer's report;
- `Task <N>: review <approved|blocking> <reviewer id> <one line>`, after a task review or scoped re-review;
- `Task <N>: codex gate round <R> <approved|blocking> <one line>`, after each per-task Codex gate round.

## Rules for every step

These hold in every step file. Where a step file and this section differ, this section governs.

- Tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE — do not re-dispatch them. Conversation memory does not survive compaction. After compaction, trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
- Dispatch implementer, task-reviewer, fix-round, re-review and final-reviewer subagents with `run_in_background: false`. Your next step always depends on the result, and a foreground call keeps your turn open, which is what an editor such as Zed shows as the session working. A background dispatch ends the turn while the subagent runs, and the editor shows the session idle.
- Run a covering command expected to finish within 10 minutes in the foreground, with an explicit timeout of at least its expected runtime and at most 600000 ms. A command that may run past 10 minutes is a tracked job; [task-loop.md](task-loop.md), "Waiting on subagents and long commands", gives its commands and watch budget.
- One implementer at a time in this session: parallel work is other sessions' (one controller per task branch); never dispatch two implementers at once here.
- Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review. The one exception is the de-minimis fix in [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md).
- The task reviewer's blocking findings and the per-task Codex gate's blocking findings form one loop with ONE shared cap of **five rounds per task**: the gate does not run a count of its own.
- When round 5's re-review — or a per-task Codex gate at the spent cap — still leaves blocking findings open, stop dispatching and surface the task as BLOCKED, as [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md) describes under the breaker.

## Model Selection

Match the model to the task's difficulty rather than defaulting. Two rules are
defaults you will get wrong by omission, so they stay here: **always specify
the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent** — an omitted model inherits
your session's, usually the most capable and most expensive — and **a mid-tier
model is the floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose
descriptions**, whatever the schedule pressure. The cheapest tier is for
transcription, where the task's own text carries the complete code to write,
and for single-file mechanical fixes. The per-role guidance, the complexity
signals, and the fix-loop escalation rule are in
[model-selection.md](model-selection.md).

## The waiting board

Before you ask your human partner a question, hand back BLOCKED, meet an
empty frontier (`held` or `blocked`), or stop on a merge conflict, post what
you wait on: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --kind
<question|tasks|merge|gate|handoff> [--task N] --note "<one line>"`, and put
the session lines of `scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE` in what you write.
When you resume, clear it: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --clear`.
The board is how your human partner finds the session that needs them among
several; a session that holds a claim and posts nothing shows as quiet
after half an hour, which is where they look for a permission prompt.

## Risk Tiers (per-task Codex gate applicability)

Tiers are `low`, `standard`, `high`, declared per task in the plan. A task
skips the per-task Codex gate only when all three hold: declared low, the
plan's own Codex gate actually reviewed the plan, and no escalation trigger
fired at any point during execution. That skip is recorded durably. An
unreviewed low tier — plan gate skipped, degraded, or outcome unknown —
executes as standard, and a task demoted that way runs the full train and
records NO tier-skip event. The Claude task reviewer and the final
whole-branch train never tier off. When any task did skip, write
`tier-skips.md` in this plan's workspace; Final Review hands its path to the
final reviewer and the final Codex gate. The escalation triggers, the
fallback rules, and the exact ledger line shape are in
[risk-tiers.md](risk-tiers.md) — read it before dispatching any task declared
low.

## Common Rationalizations

The excuses that show up mid-run and what is actually true:
[common-rationalizations.md](common-rationalizations.md). Read it the moment you
catch yourself justifying a shortcut.

## Example Workflow

A complete worked run, dispatch through finish:
[example-workflow.md](example-workflow.md).

32	    "subagent-driven-development" [shape=box];
33	    "executing-plans" [shape=box];
34	    "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [shape=box];
35	
36	    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Tasks mostly independent?" [label="yes"];
37	    "Have implementation plan?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no"];
38	    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Stay in this session?" [label="yes"];
39	    "Tasks mostly independent?" -> "Manual execution or brainstorm first" [label="no - tightly coupled"];
40	    "Stay in this session?" -> "subagent-driven-development" [label="yes"];
41	    "Stay in this session?" -> "executing-plans" [label="no - parallel session"];
42	}
43	```
44	
45	**vs. Executing Plans (parallel session):**
46	- Same session (no context switch)
47	- Fresh subagent per task (no context pollution)
48	- Review after each task (spec compliance + code quality), broad review at the end
49	- Faster iteration (no human-in-loop between tasks)
50	
51	## The Process
52	
53	Each step's full text is in its own file beside this one. Read a step's file when you enter the step; after a compaction, the step table below names the one to read.
54	
55	1. **Setup** ([setup.md](setup.md)): sync the state branch and find the plan's workspace, settle where the work happens (hyperpowers:using-git-worktrees), create or read the ledger and append your session line, verify, read the plan and the spec, run the pre-flight scan. Setup's last action appends `session <sid>: setup complete`.
56	2. **Take a task and dispatch** ([task-loop.md](task-loop.md)): `scripts/sdd-state next` offers a task; claim the first and switch to its branch (none to take, or blocked: post, print the board, hand back). Dispatch the implementer, answer its questions, handle its report.
57	3. **Review the task** ([review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md)): generate the review package and dispatch the task reviewer. Blocking findings go to step 4; a finding that conflicts with the plan text goes to your human partner first.
58	4. **Fix loop** ([fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md)): fix rounds, each with a scoped re-review, under the shared cap in the rules below. When no finding is left open, go back to review-and-complete.md for the gate.
59	5. **Codex task gate and completion** ([review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md)): unless the task's effective tier is low, run the per-task Codex gate (blocking findings re-enter step 4). Append the `approved` line, merge back, detach, delete the task branch, and run `scripts/sdd-state complete`; any status but `complete` stops. Then step 2.
60	6. **Final review and Finish** ([final-and-finish.md](final-and-finish.md)): when no task remains, claim the final train, dispatch the final reviewer (one fix dispatch, one scoped re-review), the decision extractor and the Codex final gate, delete the workspace, then use hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch.
61	
62	## After a compaction: the step table
63	
64	Print the board (`scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE`) and the ledger lines of your task and your Setup (`grep -E '^(Task <N>:|session <sid>: setup complete)' <workspace>/progress.md`, leaving out `Task <N>:` when you hold no task); `scripts/sdd-dir PLAN_FILE` prints the workspace. Do not Read the whole ledger after a compaction: it grows with the plan. A row's newest line is the newest of your task's lines the table names (its branch, base, implementer identity, `report`, `review`, Codex gate round, `approved`, `merged` and `fix round` lines); a line it does not name, such as a deferred minor or the gate directory, leaves your step unchanged. Then Read the step file this table names:
65	
66	| State | Step file |
67	|---|---|
68	| no ledger in the workspace, or no `setup complete` line of this session in it | [setup.md](setup.md) |
69	| the board shows no task held by this session and a task without a completion line | [task-loop.md](task-loop.md) |
70	| the held task's newest line is its branch, base, implementer identity or `report` line | [task-loop.md](task-loop.md) |
71	| its newest line is a `review` or Codex gate line approving it, an `approved` line or a `merged` line | [review-and-complete.md](review-and-complete.md) |
72	| its newest line is a `fix round` line, or a `review` or Codex gate line with blocking findings | [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md) |
73	| this session holds the final claim, or every task has a completion line | [final-and-finish.md](final-and-finish.md) |
74	
75	A state the table does not cover reads [task-loop.md](task-loop.md), and you record that in the ledger.
76	
77	The table reads these ledger lines, so write each one where its step says:
78	
79	- `session <sid>: setup complete`, Setup's last action;
80	- `Task <N>: report <status> <one line>`, after an implementer's report;
81	- `Task <N>: review <approved|blocking> <reviewer id> <one line>`, after a task review or scoped re-review;
82	- `Task <N>: codex gate round <R> <approved|blocking> <one line>`, after each per-task Codex gate round.
83	
84	## Rules for every step
85	
86	These hold in every step file. Where a step file and this section differ, this section governs.
87	
88	- Tasks with a `Task <N>: complete` line are DONE — do not re-dispatch them. Conversation memory does not survive compaction. After compaction, trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection.
89	- Dispatch implementer, task-reviewer, fix-round, re-review and final-reviewer subagents with `run_in_background: false`. Your next step always depends on the result, and a foreground call keeps your turn open, which is what an editor such as Zed shows as the session working. A background dispatch ends the turn while the subagent runs, and the editor shows the session idle.
90	- Run a covering command expected to finish within 10 minutes in the foreground, with an explicit timeout of at least its expected runtime and at most 600000 ms. A command that may run past 10 minutes is a tracked job; [task-loop.md](task-loop.md), "Waiting on subagents and long commands", gives its commands and watch budget.
91	- One implementer at a time in this session: parallel work is other sessions' (one controller per task branch); never dispatch two implementers at once here.
92	- Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review. The one exception is the de-minimis fix in [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md).
93	- The task reviewer's blocking findings and the per-task Codex gate's blocking findings form one loop with ONE shared cap of **five rounds per task**: the gate does not run a count of its own.
94	- When round 5's re-review — or a per-task Codex gate at the spent cap — still leaves blocking findings open, stop dispatching and surface the task as BLOCKED, as [fix-loop.md](fix-loop.md) describes under the breaker.
95	
96	## Model Selection
97	
98	Match the model to the task's difficulty rather than defaulting. Two rules are
99	defaults you will get wrong by omission, so they stay here: **always specify
100	the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent** — an omitted model inherits
101	your session's, usually the most capable and most expensive — and **a mid-tier
102	model is the floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose
103	descriptions**, whatever the schedule pressure. The cheapest tier is for
104	transcription, where the task's own text carries the complete code to write,
105	and for single-file mechanical fixes. The per-role guidance, the complexity
106	signals, and the fix-loop escalation rule are in
107	[model-selection.md](model-selection.md).
108	
109	## The waiting board
110	
111	Before you ask your human partner a question, hand back BLOCKED, meet an
112	empty frontier (`held` or `blocked`), or stop on a merge conflict, post what
113	you wait on: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --kind
114	<question|tasks|merge|gate|handoff> [--task N] --note "<one line>"`, and put
115	the session lines of `scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE` in what you write.
116	When you resume, clear it: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session <sid> --clear`.
117	The board is how your human partner finds the session that needs them among
118	several; a session that holds a claim and posts nothing shows as quiet
119	after half an hour, which is where they look for a permission prompt.
120	
121	## Risk Tiers (per-task Codex gate applicability)
122	
123	Tiers are `low`, `standard`, `high`, declared per task in the plan. A task
124	skips the per-task Codex gate only when all three hold: declared low, the
125	plan's own Codex gate actually reviewed the plan, and no escalation trigger
126	fired at any point during execution. That skip is recorded durably. An
127	unreviewed low tier — plan gate skipped, degraded, or outcome unknown —
128	executes as standard, and a task demoted that way runs the full train and
129	records NO tier-skip event. The Claude task reviewer and the final
130	whole-branch train never tier off. When any task did skip, write
131	`tier-skips.md` in this plan's workspace; Final Review hands its path to the
132	final reviewer and the final Codex gate. The escalation triggers, the
133	fallback rules, and the exact ledger line shape are in
134	[risk-tiers.md](risk-tiers.md) — read it before dispatching any task declared
135	low.
136	
137	## Common Rationalizations
138	
139	The excuses that show up mid-run and what is actually true:
140	[common-rationalizations.md](common-rationalizations.md). Read it the moment you
141	catch yourself justifying a shortcut.
142	
143	## Example Workflow
144	
145	A complete worked run, dispatch through finish:
146	[example-workflow.md](example-workflow.md).
147

Base directory for this skill: /Users/johnss51/.cache/hyperpowers/compaction-reread-notice/arms/slice/skills/finishing-a-development-branch

# Finishing a Development Branch

## Overview

**Core principle:** Record decisions and verify tests → Detect environment → Present options → Execute choice → Clean up.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the finishing-a-development-branch skill to complete this work."

**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for the test-failure report and the PR description. The option menus below are presented exactly as written.

## Step 1: Record Decisions and Verify Tests

A branch that implements a spec leaves one record per decision in the
`decisions/` directory beside the spec's directory, compiled by
`scripts/decisions-compile` in this skill's directory from the spec's
`## Decisions` list, with the plan removed in the same commit. The records
ride the branch before any merge or push, so they are staged here and
committed in Step 4 once your human partner has seen them. Work with no spec
has no records: for it, this step is the test run alone.

1. **Find the plan and the spec.** Start from the repository root:

   ```bash
   cd "$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)"
   ```

   Run this step and Step 4 from the repository root; every path below is
   repository-relative, as the compiler and the pathspec file expect. Then
   fix the fork point, in every case, because the steps below diff and
   search from it (the base branch is whatever this work forked from,
   usually named in the plan, the conversation, or the branch's upstream;
   when it is not already known, ask now, before anything below runs: "This
   branch split from <your best guess> - is that correct?"):

   ```bash
   MERGE_BASE=$(git merge-base <base-branch> HEAD)
   ```

   The subagent-driven-development hand-off names both. Otherwise read the
   branch's history, not its tree, so a plan an earlier records commit
   removed is still found:

   ```bash
   git log --diff-filter=A --name-only --format= "$MERGE_BASE"..HEAD -- '*/plans/*.md'
   ```

   Exactly one plan is the plan; read its `**Spec:**` header from the commit
   that added it (`git show <sha>:<path>`). More than one: ask your human
   partner which applies. A plan without a Spec header, or with `none`: ask
   the same way. No plan: when the branch's history added or changed a spec
   (`git log --diff-filter=AM --name-only --format= "$MERGE_BASE"..HEAD -- '*/specs/*.md'`),
   ask whether records are wanted for it, and if so there is a spec and no
   plan; when it did neither, the work is bounded: there is no spec, skip
   the extractor and go to the test run in item 3.
2. **Take a scratch directory and dry-run the compiler.** The directory
   comes from `../requesting-code-review/scripts/codex-review-dir` (one per
   finish; the extractor's output and the pathspec file `records.paths` live
   in it, whether or not an extractor is dispatched). Then
   `bash <this skill's directory>/scripts/decisions-compile <spec> --dry-run`,
   with `--plan <plan>` added when a plan was found.
   Exit 2 for a missing decisions list is the legacy-spec case: draft the
   `## Decisions` list from the spec's own text, one item per decision it
   states, show it to your human partner, and write it into the spec once
   they approve it, and commit that edit on the branch before going on (a
   docs commit of the spec alone; the compiler requires a committed spec,
   and a skip restores the spec from HEAD). Any other exit 2 names what to fix first (a spec that is
   not committed, a plan that is not a tracked and clean markdown file under
   `plans/` whose Spec header names this spec, or a `Supersedes:` problem):
   resolve it with them before going on. Keep the numbered listing for the
   extractor.
3. **Dispatch the extractor, then run the suite.** Skip the dispatch when the
   branch has no spec, when the hand-off already names an extractor (a task
   id and an output path), when the branch already carries this spec's
   records commit (`git log "$MERGE_BASE"..HEAD --fixed-strings --grep="docs: record decisions for <spec filename without -design.md>"`,
   the subject Step 4's commit uses for this spec), or
   when your harness has no tracked background subagent (then say so when
   you hand back). Otherwise compose the dispatch from
   [decision-notes-prompt.md](decision-notes-prompt.md) with the merge-base
   diff and `<dir>/decision-notes.md` as its output path, and start it in
   the background. Then run the project's full test suite (`npm test` /
   `cargo test` / `pytest` / `go test ./...`) and wait for its result in
   this turn:
   - A suite expected to finish within 10 minutes runs in the foreground,
     with an explicit timeout of at least its expected runtime and at most
     600000 ms.
   - A suite that may run longer starts through your harness's tracked
     background option (`run_in_background` on Claude Code, with a timeout
     above its expected runtime), never with a trailing `&` or `nohup`, as
     `<suite> > <dir>/suite.log 2>&1; echo $? > <dir>/suite.exit`. `<dir>`
     is the scratch directory from item 2; when item 2 was skipped, take
     one the same way now. Then wait in the foreground with repeated
     `bash <this skill's directory>/scripts/wait-exit <dir>/suite.exit --max-ms 540000`
     calls, each with a 600000 ms tool timeout: `running` means call it
     again; `exited code=0` is a green suite; any other code is a failing
     suite, read from `<dir>/suite.log`. A launch whose timeout passes with
     no exit file is a failing suite too.

   Ending the turn while the suite runs leaves an editor such as Zed
   showing the session idle, and there the result goes unreported until
   your human partner types.
4. **If tests fail**, stop a still-running extractor (TaskStop), report the
   failures and stop — the menu comes after a green suite. Nothing is
   compiled; the plan stays.

   ```
   Tests failing (<N> failures). Must fix before completing:

   [Show failures]
   ```

5. **If tests pass** and the branch has a spec, collect the extractor without
   waiting: finished, its file is the `--notes`; unfinished, stop it
   (TaskStop), compile without notes, and say so when you hand back. The spec
   must be clean before the compile (no uncommitted edits; commit or stash
   them), because a skip restores it from HEAD. A spec that already carries
   an Outcome line is a spec another plan finished first; the compiler
   recompiles it, adding this plan to the Outcome line and its notes as
   their own paragraph. It refuses three cases, each with exit 2 and nothing
   written: this plan has the file name of a plan the spec already records;
   notes from a finish without a plan would replace notes plans wrote; or
   this plan's notes would replace notes a finish without a plan wrote. Show
   the stderr line and stop. When the hand-off names a
   dossier (SDD), first record where the board and the lease find the plan,
   because the compile removes the plan file and can empty its directory,
   and Step 6 can remove this worktree. `PLAN_REPO` is the main checkout of
   the plan's repository: it survives Step 6, and it is the plan repository
   even when the code lives in another one. `PLAN_REL` is the plan's path
   inside that repository. Both are asked from the plan's nearest existing
   directory, so a finish restarted after an earlier records commit records
   the same values (an SDD branch with no spec runs no compile and records
   them the same way before Step 4). `<plan>` in the lease commands below is
   `"$PLAN_REPO/$PLAN_REL"`.

   ```bash
   dir=$(dirname <plan>); rest=$(basename <plan>)
   while [ ! -d "$dir" ]; do rest="$(basename "$dir")/$rest"; dir=$(dirname "$dir"); done
   PLAN_REPO=$(git -C "$dir" worktree list --porcelain | sed -n '1s/^worktree //p')
   PLAN_REL=$(git -C "$dir" rev-parse --show-prefix)$rest
   ```

   Then run
   `bash <this skill's directory>/scripts/decisions-compile <spec> --plan <plan> --notes <file> --paths-file <dir>/records.paths`,
   omitting `--plan` when the branch has no plan and `--notes` when there is
   no notes file. A `notes ignored:` line on its stderr is repeated verbatim
   when you hand back. On exit 2, resolve the named problem and re-run; on
   exit 3, report the git failure and re-run once it is cleared. Nothing is
   committed here; the staged set waits for Step 4. Continue to Step 2.

## Step 2: Detect Environment

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
# Capture now, while still inside the workspace — Step 5 changes directory
# before cleanup (Step 6) needs this value
WORKTREE_PATH=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)
```

The skill that called you may pass the session's mode (`current-branch`,
`new-branch`, or `worktree`): subagent-driven-development reads it from the
ledger's `session` line before the workspace is finished, executing-plans
carries it from the branch question. A passed `new-branch` or `worktree`
changes nothing here: the environment rows below govern them as they do
today. A passed `current-branch` selects one of the two `current-branch`
rows and the environment rows do not apply to it; on the default branch it
also skips Step 3 and Step 6, on any other branch Step 3 and Step 6 run as
for the standard menu.
The repository's default branch is the branch `refs/remotes/origin/HEAD`
points at when that ref exists; otherwise whichever one of `main` and
`master` exists as a local branch; when both exist, the one
`init.defaultBranch` names, and when it names neither, ask your human
partner which is the default before choosing a row; when neither exists,
the `init.defaultBranch` value, otherwise `master`:

```bash
CURRENT_BRANCH=$(git branch --show-current)
DEFAULT_BRANCH=$(git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD 2>/dev/null | sed 's|^origin/||')
if [ -z "$DEFAULT_BRANCH" ]; then
  HAVE_MAIN=$(git show-ref --verify -q refs/heads/main && echo yes) || true
  HAVE_MASTER=$(git show-ref --verify -q refs/heads/master && echo yes) || true
  CONFIGURED=$(git config --get init.defaultBranch) || true
  if [ "$HAVE_MAIN" = yes ] && [ "$HAVE_MASTER" = yes ]; then
    case "$CONFIGURED" in main|master) DEFAULT_BRANCH=$CONFIGURED ;; *) DEFAULT_BRANCH="" ;; esac
  elif [ "$HAVE_MAIN" = yes ]; then DEFAULT_BRANCH=main
  elif [ "$HAVE_MASTER" = yes ]; then DEFAULT_BRANCH=master
  else DEFAULT_BRANCH=${CONFIGURED:-master}
  fi
fi
# An empty DEFAULT_BRANCH here means both branches exist and the config
# names neither: ask before choosing a row.
```

This determines which menu to show and how cleanup works:

| State | Menu | Cleanup |
|-------|------|---------|
| `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON` (normal repo) | Standard 3 options | No worktree to clean up |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, named branch | Standard 3 options | Provenance-based (see Step 6) |
| `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON`, detached HEAD | Reduced 2 options (no merge) | Externally managed — leave in place |
| mode `current-branch` passed, `$CURRENT_BRANCH` is `$DEFAULT_BRANCH` | Reduced 2 options (push, keep) | None: no branch and no worktree were created |
| mode `current-branch` passed, any other branch | Standard 3 options | Option 1 deletes the merged branch as usual; no worktree to remove |
| `$DEFAULT_BRANCH` is empty (both `main` and `master` exist, `init.defaultBranch` names neither) | Ask your human partner which is the default, then read this table again | Decided by the row their answer selects |

## Step 3: Determine Base Branch

Skip this step when mode `current-branch` was passed and `$CURRENT_BRANCH`
is `$DEFAULT_BRANCH`: there is no merge and no base to confirm. A
`current-branch` session on any other branch needs its base like any
feature branch.

The base branch is the one Step 1 confirmed: whatever this work forked
from, usually named in the plan, the conversation, or the branch's
upstream. When Step 1 had no spec and did not ask, confirm it here the same
way (ask "This branch split from <your best guess> - is that correct?").
Confirm before merging: merging into the wrong base is expensive to undo.

## Step 4: Present Options

**When Step 1 staged records,** the message that presents the options, from
the repository root as in Step 1, opens
with the complete staged diff over the pathspec file's paths (`git diff` has
no pathspec-file option, so the NUL-delimited file is read into an array; a
path with a space survives, and the variable makes the entries literal, as
the compiler's own git calls are, so a bracket or star in a spec name
matches only itself):

```bash
PATHS_FILE=<dir>/records.paths
paths=(); while IFS= read -r -d '' p; do paths+=("$p"); done < "$PATHS_FILE"
GIT_LITERAL_PATHSPECS=1 git diff --cached -- "${paths[@]}"
```

The message carries that command's output itself, verbatim; a summary, a
list of paths or a pointer to a tool result is not the diff, and no option is
accepted until the diff has been shown. Then the extractor's proposals from
its notes file, each with the question
it needs: an undocumented decision (add it to the spec's `## Decisions`
list, or dismiss it); a proposed supersession (add a
`Supersedes: <record path>` line to the item that reverses that record, or
dismiss it); then one line offering to skip the records for this branch; and
only then the menu text exactly as written below. Your human partner answers
once. An answer that names an option but leaves any proposal without a
disposition is incomplete: ask for the missing dispositions and wait; nothing
is written or committed until every proposal has one. A skip is settled
before any accepted proposal is written: an answer that both accepts a
proposal and skips is incomplete, so ask which they mean. Unless they chose
the skip, before executing their option: write each accepted proposal into the spec (an accepted undocumented
decision is appended after the list's last item, never inserted, so the
numbers the notes use stay with their records; an accepted supersession is a
`Supersedes:` line on the item it belongs to),
then re-run the compiler with the same arguments (it stages the spec,
carrying the proposal and the Outcome line, with the records and the index),
and because the staged set
changed, show the new complete staged diff and ask only for its approval,
not the dispositions again; record a dismissal in the hand-back in their
words. An approval leads to the one records commit below, which takes the
spec too through the pathspec file; a withheld approval commits nothing,
keeps the staged set and the spec edit in place, and asks what to change (the
skip was settled before any proposal was written, so `--undo` is not this
path's tool). If they change their mind to a skip at that point, first take
the accepted proposal back out of the spec and stage the spec again
(`GIT_LITERAL_PATHSPECS=1 git add -- <spec>`), so `--undo` sees no later edit; record the proposal's
text in the hand-back, so their words are not lost; then follow the skip
path. A skip ends the records for this branch:
run `bash <this skill's directory>/scripts/decisions-compile --undo <spec> --plan <plan>` (without `--plan` when there
is none), record it in their words, make no commit, and run the option they
chose. Otherwise commit:

```bash
GIT_LITERAL_PATHSPECS=1 git commit --pathspec-from-file=<dir>/records.paths --pathspec-file-nul -m "docs: record decisions for <spec filename without -design.md>"
```

The message is that one line and nothing else: no second `-m`, no trailer, no
attribution or `Co-Authored-By` line, whatever the harness suggests. An empty
pathspec file means there is nothing to commit (the branch already carries
its records): skip the commit and run the chosen option.

The option runs only after that commit succeeds. If it fails (a hook, an
index conflict, anything), show the failure, stop, and run the same commit
again once the cause is cleared; nothing is merged or pushed while the
records and the plan's deletion are merely staged.

Then run the option they chose. A branch with no records shows the menu as it
always did.

**Plans that share the integration branch.** When the hand-off names a
dossier (SDD), run `bash <this skill's directory>/../subagent-driven-development/scripts/sdd-state board --repo "$PLAN_REPO"`:
`PLAN_REPO` is the main checkout of the plan file's repository, recorded in
Step 1 before the compile, where the dossier lives, which is not the code
repository when the plan lives elsewhere. When it lists
another open plan whose `integration=` is this branch, the merge option is
withheld. The withheld-merge line replaces option 1 only in a menu that
offers a merge: present the three-option menu with option 1 replaced by the
line `1. (merge withheld: plan <ws> is still open on this branch)` and
accept only options 2 and 3. The two-option menus (mode `current-branch` on
the default branch, and a detached HEAD) have no merge option and are shown
unchanged. In every menu, say which plan is open, and a pull request's
description states that another plan is still open on the branch.

**Normal repo and named-branch worktree — present exactly these 3 options:**

```
Implementation complete. What would you like to do?

1. Merge back to <base-branch> locally
2. Push and create a Pull Request
3. Keep the branch as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

**Mode `current-branch` on the default branch — present exactly these 2 options:**

```
Implementation complete on <branch>. What would you like to do?

1. Push <branch>
2. Keep as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

**Detached HEAD — present exactly these 2 options:**

```
Implementation complete. You're on a detached HEAD (externally managed workspace).

1. Push as new branch and create a Pull Request
2. Keep as-is (I'll handle it later)

Which option?
```

Present the menu exactly as written — concise, with every option coming
from the list above. Discarding the work happens only in response to your
human partner explicitly asking for it (see "If your human partner asks to
discard the work" below). Wait for their answer; the integration decision
is theirs.

## Step 5: Execute Choice

### Mode current-branch on the default branch

The two-option menu above maps to: option 1 pushes exactly this branch,
`git push <remote> <branch>:<branch>` (add `-u` when the branch has no

skills.name: hyperpowers:using-git-worktrees
skills.content:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/johnss51/.cache/hyperpowers/compaction-reread-notice/arms/slice/skills/using-git-worktrees

# Using Git Worktrees

## Overview

Settle where the work happens: detect an existing isolated workspace, otherwise ask your human partner to choose between the current branch, a new branch in place, and an isolated worktree, and report the mode. When the answer is a worktree, prefer your platform's native worktree tools and fall back to manual git worktrees only when no native tool is available.

**Core principle:** Detect existing isolation first. Then use native tools. Then fall back to git. Never fight the harness.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the using-git-worktrees skill to settle where the work happens."

## Step 0: Detect Existing Isolation

**Before creating anything, check if you are already in an isolated workspace.**

```bash
GIT_DIR=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
GIT_COMMON=$(cd "$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)" 2>/dev/null && pwd -P)
BRANCH=$(git branch --show-current)
```

**Submodule guard:** `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON` is also true inside git submodules. Before concluding "already in a worktree," verify you are not in a submodule:

```bash
# If this returns a path, you're in a submodule, not a worktree — treat as normal repo
git rev-parse --show-superproject-working-tree 2>/dev/null
```

**If `GIT_DIR != GIT_COMMON` (and not a submodule):** You are already in a linked worktree. Skip to Step 2 (Project Setup), after the detach in Detaching a later session (every path) when this is a later session of a running SDD plan. Do NOT create another worktree.
The mode is `worktree`; report it with the branch state below.

Report with branch state:
- On a branch: "Already in isolated workspace at `<path>` on branch `<name>`."
- Detached HEAD: "Already in isolated workspace at `<path>` (detached HEAD, externally managed). Branch creation needed at finish time."

**If `GIT_DIR == GIT_COMMON` (or in a submodule):** You are in a normal repo checkout.

Has your human partner already declared where this work should happen (an
instruction file naming a worktree, a new branch, or the current branch)?
If so, honor it without asking. Otherwise ask one question with exactly
these three options, in this order (on Claude Code use the selection
widget; elsewhere ask in plain text):

1. Stay on the current branch (`<current branch>`)
2. Create a new branch in place (`git switch -c <name>`; the name from the
   plan slug unless they give one)
3. Create an isolated worktree

The answer is the mode (`current-branch`, `new-branch`, or `worktree`); the
skill that called you records it in its ledger. Choosing "stay on the
current branch" is explicit consent to work there, main or master included.
For option 1 skip to Step 2; for option 2 create the branch, then skip to
Step 2; for option 3 continue with Step 1. Report the mode in every case.

## Step 1: Create Isolated Workspace

**You have two mechanisms. Try them in this order.**

### 1a. Native Worktree Tools (preferred)

Your human partner chose a worktree in Step 0. Do you already have a way to create one? It might be a tool with a name like `EnterWorktree`, `WorktreeCreate`, a `/worktree` command, or a `--worktree` flag. If you do, use it and skip to Step 2, after the detach in Detaching a later session (every path) when this is a later session of a running SDD plan. If the tool is denied or fails, do not fall through to `git worktree add` and do not continue in the current checkout on your own: ask the Step 0 question again with options 1 and 2 only, and report that answer as the mode. The mode is `worktree` only once a worktree exists.

Native tools handle directory placement, branch creation, and cleanup automatically. Using `git worktree add` when you have a native tool creates phantom state your harness can't see or manage.

Only proceed to Step 1b if you have no native worktree tool available.

### 1b. Git Worktree Fallback

**Only use this if Step 1a does not apply** — you have no native worktree tool available. Create a worktree manually using git.

#### Directory Selection

Follow this priority order. Explicit user preference always beats observed filesystem state.

1. **Check your instructions for a declared worktree directory preference.** If the user has already specified one, use it without asking.

2. **Check for an existing project-local worktree directory:**
   ```bash
   ls -d .worktrees 2>/dev/null     # Preferred (hidden)
   ls -d worktrees 2>/dev/null      # Alternative
   ```
   If found, use it. If both exist, `.worktrees` wins.

3. **If there is no other guidance available**, default to `.worktrees/` at the project root.

#### Safety Verification (project-local directories only)

**MUST verify directory is ignored before creating worktree:**

```bash
git check-ignore -q .worktrees 2>/dev/null || git check-ignore -q worktrees 2>/dev/null
```

**If NOT ignored:** Add to .gitignore, commit the change, then proceed.

**Why critical:** Prevents accidentally committing worktree contents to repository.

#### Create the Worktree

```bash
# Determine path based on chosen location
path="$LOCATION/$BRANCH_NAME"

git worktree add "$path" -b "$BRANCH_NAME"
cd "$path"
```

**A later session of a plan that is already running** (the SDD skill says
so: the plan's ledger has a plan line naming an integration branch) starts
its worktree detached at that branch's head rather than on a new branch:

```bash
path="$LOCATION/<integration branch>-<session id>"
git worktree add --detach "$path" "<integration branch>"
cd "$path"
```

The path carries the session id (the `<sid>` the SDD skill uses) because the
first session's worktree normally still exists at `$LOCATION/<integration branch>`.

The integration branch itself is checked out nowhere while sessions work on
the plan; the claim creates the task branch and the controller checks it
out, and after each merge-back the worktree detaches again at the merged
head.

**Detaching a later session (every path).** An existing linked worktree
(Step 0), a native tool's worktree (Step 1a) and work in place do not go
through the block above. A later session of a running SDD plan then detaches
at the integration head before the plan's first claim:

```bash
git switch --detach "<integration branch>"
```

The SDD skill names the integration branch (the plan line of its ledger) and
runs this once it has read that line, which is after Steps 0-1 here, so a
branch the native tool created is simply left unused. The Step 0 and Step 1a
skips above are not exceptions: a later session of a running SDD plan then
detaches it; see Detaching a later session (every path).

Before that detach, and before any claim, the later session compares
`git rev-parse --show-toplevel` with the `at <toplevel>` of every other
session's newest session line in the plan's ledger. A match means it is
inside another session's worktree (a native tool can resume one under the
same name, and work in place shares that session's checkout): it must not
detach, switch or claim there. It leaves that worktree (your platform's
workspace-exit tool, where it has one) and creates its own, with a name that
carries its session id (`<integration branch>-<session id>`, passed to the
native tool or used as the Step 1b path above), then detaches that one.

**Sandbox fallback:** If `git worktree add` fails with a permission error (sandbox denial), tell your human partner the sandbox blocked worktree creation and ask the Step 0 question again with options 1 and 2 only. Their answer is the mode you report (`current-branch` or `new-branch`); a denied worktree is never reported as `worktree`. Then run setup and baseline tests in place.

## Step 2: Project Setup

Auto-detect and run appropriate setup:

```bash
# Node.js
if [ -f package.json ]; then npm install; fi

# Rust
if [ -f Cargo.toml ]; then cargo build; fi

# Python
if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
if [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then poetry install; fi

# Go
if [ -f go.mod ]; then go mod download; fi
```

## Step 3: Verify Clean Baseline

Run tests to ensure workspace starts clean:

```bash
# Use project-appropriate command
npm test / cargo test / pytest / go test ./...
```

**If tests fail:** Report failures, ask whether to proceed or investigate.

**If tests pass:** Report ready.

### Report

```
<Worktree ready at <full-path> | Working in place on <branch>>
Mode: <current-branch|new-branch|worktree>
Tests passing (<N> tests, 0 failures)
Ready to implement <feature-name>
```

The first line claims a worktree only under mode `worktree`; under
`current-branch` and `new-branch` none was created, so name the branch the
work is happening on instead. The mode line is never omitted: the skill
that called you records it, and the finishing skill routes on it.

## Quick Reference

| Situation | Action |
|-----------|--------|
| Already in linked worktree | Skip creation (Step 0) |
| Declared preference in instructions | Honor it, no question (Step 0) |
| No declared preference | Ask the three-way question (Step 0) |
| Answer: current branch | Work in place, mode `current-branch` |
| Answer: new branch | `git switch -c <name>`, mode `new-branch` |
| Answer: worktree | Step 1, mode `worktree` |
| In a submodule | Treat as normal repo (Step 0 guard) |
| Native worktree tool available | Use it (Step 1a) |
| Native tool denied or failed | Re-ask options 1 and 2; their answer is the mode, never `worktree` (Step 1a) |
| No native tool | Git worktree fallback (Step 1b) |
| `.worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| `worktrees/` exists | Use it (verify ignored) |
| Both exist | Use `.worktrees/` |
| Later session on a running SDD plan | Detached worktree at the integration head (Step 1b) |
| Later session with an existing, native or in-place workspace | `git switch --detach "<integration branch>"` before the first claim (Detaching a later session) |
| Later session whose toplevel is another session's in the ledger | Do not detach, switch or claim there; leave it, create a worktree named with your session id, detach that one (Detaching a later session) |
| Neither exists | Check instruction file, then default `.worktrees/` |
| Directory not ignored | Add to .gitignore + commit |
| Permission error on create | Re-ask options 1 and 2; their answer is the mode, never `worktree` (Step 1b) |
| Tests fail during baseline | Report failures + ask |
| No package.json/Cargo.toml | Skip dependency install |

## Common Rationalizations

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "I'm obviously not in a worktree — no need to check" | Run Step 0. Harness-created isolation and submodules both fool eyeballing; the detection commands settle it. |
| "`git worktree add` is quicker than hunting for a native tool" | A native tool (e.g. `EnterWorktree`) owns placement, branching, and cleanup. Bypassing it is the #1 mistake — it creates phantom state your harness can't see or manage. |
| "The worktree directory is surely ignored already" | Run `git check-ignore`. An unignored worktree directory commits the whole tree into the repo. |
| "Any directory name works" | Explicit instructions beat an existing project-local directory, which beats the `.worktrees/` default. |
| "The workspace is fresh — baseline tests can wait" | A dirty baseline makes every later failure ambiguous. Run the tests now; proceeding past failures is your human partner's call. |
| "They said current branch, so the consent rule does not apply to me" | It applies; that answer is the consent. Record the mode and work there; never switch branches on your own. |
